newsitem.title: UK: British markets downbeat as stg goes into reversal.
newsitem.headline: British markets downbeat as stg goes into reversal.

text.p: - British financial markets suffered on Friday as a corrective slump in the country's currency added to pressure on shares and bonds.

The FTSE 100 index of leading shares had been storming away in recent days and weeks, but with shaky financial markets in the U.S. and a fast-falling pound, the index declined more than one percent on Friday.
Sterling, knocked by the perception British monetary authorities now want a lower pound, skidded another five pfennigs and futures on British gilts were down almost a full point.

"We've been taking money out of sterling for a while," said Ian Carstairs, head of UK equities at Invesco in London. "We've also been continuing to take some money out of UK equities. That's gone abroad into bonds."
The pound, which dropped as low as 2.9150 marks on Friday, has fallen more than 12 pfennigs in the past week and 17 pfennigs from its recent eight-year peak of 3.0878 marks.
"The pace of the fall has been amazing....But there is still scope on the downside and we could possibly go back to 2.90-marks," said Audrey Childe-Freeman, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Sterling's decline has been as swift as its rise and dealers said the move was encouraged by the Bank of England's latest monetary decisions.

While the central bank on Thursday raised interest rates for the fourth time in as many months -- normally a positive factor for a currency -- it also said rates were at levels consistent with the government's inflation targets.
"The sterling bubble has well and truly burst," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN AMRO in London.

Carstairs said a positive sign from the week's events was that the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee was not overly aggressive in trying to meet the inflation target, at the risk of slamming the brakes on the economy.

Also, he said the pound's setback meant the divergence between small to mid-cap shares and blue chips could start to be reversed. With a greater concentration of exporters, shares in medium-sized companies were more exposed to movements in sterling.
He said Invesco had been overweight in British shares and its reduced allocation was to address that.
Sterling at 1600 GMT was at 2.9265 marks and $1.5850, down from previous European closes of around 2.97 marks and $1.5880.
The FTSE 100 finished at 5,031.3, down 55.5 points. In the week it still managed a rise of around 130 points. September gilt futures on LIFFE were down 28/32 at 114-09.
British markets face a heavy slate of economic news in the week ahead, with producer price numbers on Monday, retail prices on Tuesday, and unemployment and average earnings figures on Wednesday.
Also on Wednesday is a Bank of England (BOE) inflation report and minutes of a BOE meeting.
